title: Kinds of chemical reactions: joining, splitting, swapping and burning

summary.text: Squeeze lemon into milk and curds form, and a second squeeze makes no more. Why does it stop? In this unit you will find out which ran out, heat a powder to see if it splits, and build one reaction each of four kinds.
summary.art: A steel bowl of hot milk with white curds forming where a child squeezes half a lemon over it, and a small cup of fresh milk waiting beside the bowl.

intro.hook: A cook squeezes lemon juice into hot milk to make paneer. The milk was a liquid, and the lemon juice was a liquid. So where did the solid curds come from?
intro.text: The curds were in the milk all along, as tiny clusters too small to see. The acid in the lemon juice changed them, so they stuck together and came out as a solid. That is one kind of chemical reaction. In this unit you meet four kinds. In a joining reaction, two substances become one. In a splitting reaction, one substance becomes two or more. In a swapping reaction, substances exchange parts. In burning, a fuel reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light. You make curds, heat baking soda under a cold lid, mix plaster and shake soap with vinegar.
intro.art: A kitchen counter with four small scenes in a row: plaster setting in a paper cup, white powder in a pan under a steel lid, a bowl of curds and whey, and a candle flame.

outcomes: I can say what reactants and products are, and that a reaction breaks old bonds and makes new ones.
I can describe a joining reaction, and give plaster and water as an example.
I can describe a splitting reaction, and say what heat does to baking soda.
I can describe a swapping reaction, and say what vinegar does to soap.
I can explain why lemon juice makes curds in milk, and what a precipitate is.
I can describe burning as a fuel reacting with oxygen, giving out heat and light.
I can explain why a reaction stops when one reactant is used up.
I can sort a reaction into its kind, and say when one reaction fits two kinds.

terms.meaning: A change in which substances turn into new substances. The atoms stay the same, but they end up with new partners.
terms.example: Lemon juice and hot milk react. They make curds and whey, which are new substances.
terms.art: Two cups labelled 'before' pouring into one bowl labelled 'after', with the contents of the bowl looking different from both cups.

terms.meaning: A substance that you start with in a reaction. It is used up as the reaction goes on.
terms.example: In making curds, the reactants are the milk protein and the acid in lemon juice.
terms.art: A glass of milk and half a lemon on the left of an arrow.

terms.meaning: A new substance that a reaction makes.
terms.example: When plaster of Paris sets, the product is a hard solid called gypsum.
terms.art: An arrow pointing to a hard white block that has been tipped out of a paper cup.

terms.meaning: The hold between two atoms that are joined. A reaction breaks some bonds and makes new ones.
terms.example: In water, one oxygen atom has a bond to each of two hydrogen atoms.
terms.art: One large ball joined to two small balls by short sticks, as a model of a water molecule.

terms.meaning: A reaction in which two or more substances become one new substance. Chemists also call it a combination reaction.
terms.example: Plaster of Paris and water join and become one hard solid.
terms.art: Two different shapes on the left of an arrow, and the same two shapes locked together as one piece on the right.

terms.meaning: A reaction in which one substance becomes two or more new substances. Chemists also call it a decomposition reaction.
terms.example: Heat splits baking soda into washing soda, water and carbon dioxide.
terms.art: One piece made of three locked shapes on the left of an arrow, and the three shapes lying apart on the right.

terms.meaning: A reaction in which substances exchange parts. Chemists also call it a displacement reaction.
terms.example: Soap and vinegar swap parts. They make a white fatty solid and a salt that stays dissolved.
terms.art: Two pairs of dancers on the left of an arrow, and the same four dancers with changed partners on the right.

terms.meaning: A fast reaction between a fuel and oxygen that gives out heat and light. Chemists also call it combustion.
terms.example: Candle wax burns with oxygen from the air and makes carbon dioxide and water.
terms.art: A candle flame with arrows of air coming in at the base and arrows of gas rising from the top.

terms.meaning: A substance that can burn. Most fuels contain carbon and hydrogen.
terms.example: Wax, wood, cooking gas, petrol and dry leaves are fuels.
terms.art: A candle, a small pile of firewood, a gas cylinder and a dry leaf in a row.

terms.meaning: A solid that forms inside a liquid during a reaction. It forms because one product does not dissolve in water.
terms.example: The white bits that appear when vinegar is added to soap water are a precipitate.
terms.art: A clear glass of liquid with a cloud of white specks forming in the middle and settling slowly.

terms.meaning: The soft white solid that comes out of milk when an acid is added. Curds are mostly milk protein and fat.
terms.example: Paneer is made by pressing the curds from hot milk and lemon juice.
terms.art: A cloth strainer holding soft white lumps over a steel bowl.

terms.meaning: The thin, pale yellow-green liquid left after the curds come out of milk. It is mostly water, with milk sugar and minerals.
terms.example: After paneer is strained, the liquid left in the bowl is whey.
terms.art: A steel bowl of thin, pale yellow-green liquid beside a strainer of white curds.

terms.meaning: The main protein in milk. It floats in milk as tiny clusters that are too small to see.
terms.example: Lemon juice makes the casein clusters stick together, and they become curds.
terms.art: A circle showing a zoomed-in view of milk, with many tiny round clusters floating apart from each other.

terms.meaning: A reactant is used up when none of it is left to react. Then the reaction stops.
terms.example: Once all the casein has become curds, more lemon juice makes no more curds.
terms.art: An empty cup beside a half-full cup, with a full stop sign between them.

terms.meaning: A white powder made by heating a rock called gypsum. Mixed with water, it joins with the water and sets hard.
terms.example: Doctors use plaster of Paris for casts, and artists use it for statues.
terms.art: A bag of fine white powder beside a hard white cast of a hand.

terms.meaning: A short way to write a reaction in words. The reactants go before the arrow and the products go after it.
terms.art: A notebook line reading 'plaster of Paris + water → gypsum' in a child's handwriting.

explanations.concept: A reaction breaks old bonds and makes new ones
explanations.definition: A chemical reaction is a change in which substances turn into new substances. Bonds between atoms break, and new bonds form.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms. In most substances the atoms are joined to each other, and each join is called a bond. In a chemical reaction, some bonds break and new bonds form. The atoms themselves do not change, and none is made or lost. They only end up with new partners. The substances you start with are the reactants. The new substances are the products. Breaking a bond takes energy in. Making a bond gives energy out. That is why some reactions feel warm and others need heating. There are millions of known reactions. Chemists sort them into kinds by what the atoms do. This unit uses four kinds: joining, splitting, swapping and burning.
examples: Milk protein and lemon acid are reactants. Curds and whey are products.
When plaster sets, new bonds form, and the cup feels warm.
Baking soda splits only when heat is put in.
explanations.art: A row of balls joined in pairs on the left, loose balls in the middle, and the same balls joined in new pairs on the right.

explanations.definition: In a joining reaction, two or more substances join and make one new substance. Chemists call it a combination reaction.
explanations.description: The pattern of a joining reaction is A + B → AB. Plaster of Paris is a good example. The powder and the water join, and the product is one solid called gypsum. The water does not dry away. It becomes part of the solid, which is why plaster sets hard while it is still wet. Rusting is a joining reaction too. Iron joins with oxygen and water, and the product is rust. Joining reactions make new bonds, so many of them give out heat. A cup of setting plaster feels warm. Quicklime joins with water so strongly that the water can boil. Lime plaster on a wall slowly joins with carbon dioxide from the air, and turns hard.
examples: Plaster of Paris + water → gypsum.
Iron + oxygen + water → rust.
Quicklime + water → slaked lime, which is the chuna used in whitewash.
explanations.art: A paper cup of white paste with wavy lines of warmth rising from it, and a child's hand touching the outside of the cup.

explanations.concept: Splitting: one substance becomes two or more
explanations.definition: In a splitting reaction, one substance breaks into two or more new substances. Chemists call it a decomposition reaction.
explanations.description: The pattern of a splitting reaction is AB → A + B. Bonds must break, so many splitting reactions need energy put in. The energy can be heat, electricity or light. Heat splits baking soda into three substances: washing soda, water and carbon dioxide. The water leaves as steam, and the carbon dioxide leaves as a gas. That gas is what makes a cake or a dhokla rise. Electricity splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. Heat splits seashells and limestone into quicklime and carbon dioxide. Splitting is the opposite of joining. Heat drives the water out of gypsum and makes plaster of Paris. Adding water joins them again.
examples: Baking soda, heated → washing soda + water + carbon dioxide.
Water, with electricity → hydrogen + oxygen.
Limestone, heated strongly → quicklime + carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: A small steel pan of white powder on a low flame, with a steel lid held above it and drops of water on the underside of the lid.

explanations.definition: In a swapping reaction, substances exchange parts and make new substances. Chemists call it a displacement reaction.
explanations.description: The pattern of a swapping reaction is AB + CD → AD + CB. Each substance has two parts, and the parts change partners. Soap is made of a long fatty part joined to sodium. Vinegar is an acid, and an acid has hydrogen to give. When they meet, the sodium and the hydrogen change places. The fatty part with hydrogen is a waxy solid that does not dissolve, so the water turns milky. The sodium ends up in a salt that stays dissolved. Sometimes only one part moves. An iron nail in blue copper sulphate water slowly gets a brown coat of copper. The iron takes the place of the copper.
examples: Soap + vinegar → a white fatty solid + a dissolved salt.
Stomach acid + an antacid → a salt + water.
Iron + copper sulphate → copper + iron sulphate.
explanations.art: Two pairs of joined shapes, a circle with a square and a triangle with a star, and after an arrow the circle with the star and the triangle with the square.

explanations.concept: Precipitation: why milk and lemon make curds
explanations.definition: Precipitation is the forming of a solid inside a liquid during a reaction. The solid is called a precipitate.
explanations.description: Milk looks like one smooth liquid, but it is water with many things in it. The main protein, casein, floats as tiny clusters. Each cluster carries a small electric charge of the same kind. Charges of the same kind repel, so the clusters push each other away and stay spread out. An acid gives hydrogen to the clusters, and the hydrogen cancels their charge. Some calcium leaves the clusters and goes into the liquid. Now nothing keeps the clusters apart. They stick together, trap the fat, and come out as curds. The curds are a precipitate. Hot milk curdles with less acid than cold milk. Sour milk curdles in the same way, because bacteria in the milk have made an acid.
examples: Hot milk + lemon juice → curds + whey.
Soap + hard water → a grey scum on the bucket.
Dripping water in a cave leaves solid limestone behind, which grows into a stalactite.
explanations.art: Two zoomed-in circles: in the first, tiny round clusters float apart in milk, and in the second, the clusters have clumped into one large lump with clear liquid around it.

explanations.concept: Burning: a fuel reacts with oxygen
explanations.definition: Burning is a fast reaction between a fuel and oxygen. It gives out heat and light. Chemists call it combustion.
explanations.description: A fuel is a substance that can burn. Wax, wood, cooking gas and petrol are fuels, and they are made mostly of carbon and hydrogen. When a fuel burns, its bonds break. The carbon joins with oxygen and makes carbon dioxide. The hydrogen joins with oxygen and makes water, which leaves as steam. These new bonds are very strong, so burning gives out a lot of energy. Burning needs three things: a fuel, oxygen and enough heat to start. Water, sand and ash do not burn, because their atoms are already joined with oxygen. Your cells also react sugar with oxygen and make carbon dioxide and water. They do it in many small steps, with no flame.
examples: Wax + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with heat and light.
Cooking gas + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Hydrogen + oxygen → water. Some rocket engines burn hydrogen.
explanations.art: A candle flame with a label 'fuel' at the wax, 'oxygen' at arrows of air, and 'carbon dioxide and water' at arrows rising above the flame.

explanations.concept: A reaction stops when one reactant is used up
explanations.definition: A reaction goes on only while every reactant is present. When one reactant is used up, the reaction stops, however much of the others is left.
explanations.description: Reactants are used in fixed amounts. A cup of milk holds a fixed amount of casein. Once all of the casein has become curds, extra lemon juice has nothing to work on. The leftover acid stays in the whey. If fresh milk is added, the leftover acid makes new curds, until the acid is used up too. The reactant that runs out first decides how much product is made. Chemists call it the limiting reactant. A candle under a glass goes out for the same reason: the oxygen runs low while wax is still left. Cooks, medicine makers and factory engineers all measure reactants, so that little is wasted.
examples: More lemon in whey makes no new curds, because the casein is used up.
A candle under a glass goes out with wax still left.
Baking soda that has been fully heated gives no more water when it is heated again.
explanations.art: Two tumblers of pale whey side by side, one with lemon juice being added and staying clear, the other with milk being added and forming white flecks.

explanations.concept: One reaction can fit two kinds
explanations.description: The four kinds are a way of sorting, and some reactions fit two kinds. A burning candle is an example. The wax comes apart, and its atoms join with oxygen. So this one burning reaction is a splitting and a joining at the same time. When hydrogen burns, two substances become one, so it is a burning and a joining at once. Vinegar and baking soda first swap parts. One product, carbonic acid, then splits into water and carbon dioxide, which makes the fizz. People who study chemistry do not all sort reactions in the same way.
examples: Hydrogen + oxygen → water is both burning and joining.
Vinegar and baking soda swap parts, and then one product splits.
Heating gypsum splits off water. Adding water joins the two again.

perspectives.explanation: They sort reactions by their pattern: joining, splitting, swapping and burning. The pattern is easy to see in a word equation, and it helps you guess the products.
They sort reactions by what moves between the substances. In some reactions electrons move, and in others hydrogen moves. By this sorting, burning and rusting are the same kind.

perspectives.who: Chemists who study how reactions happen
perspectives.explanation: They say every reaction is a chain of small steps. In each step a bond breaks or a bond forms. For them, the kinds are names for common chains of steps.

explanations.art: A sorting tray with four sections labelled joining, splitting, swapping and burning, and one card lying across the line between two sections.

explanations.concept: The four kinds inside living bodies
explanations.definition: Living cells run thousands of reactions every second. Most of them are joining, splitting or swapping reactions.
explanations.description: Your body uses every kind of reaction in this unit. Digestion is mostly splitting. Long chains of starch and protein are cut into small units, and each cut uses one water molecule. Growing is mostly joining. Your cells join small units into long chains of protein, and so build muscle, skin and hair. Your cells also react sugar with oxygen. The products are the same as in burning: carbon dioxide and water. Plants do the reverse. A green leaf joins carbon dioxide and water into sugar, using the energy of light, and gives out oxygen. Living beings make precipitates too. A clam builds their shell from calcium and carbon dioxide dissolved in sea water. Your bone cells lay down a hard solid from substances dissolved in your blood.
examples: Starch + water → sugar, in your mouth and gut.
Carbon dioxide + water, with light → sugar + oxygen, in a leaf.
A hen builds the shell of each egg from calcium dissolved in her blood.
explanations.art: A child eating a banana beside a potted plant in sunlight, with arrows showing oxygen going from the plant to the child and carbon dioxide going back.

explanations.concept: The four kinds on the Earth and in space
explanations.definition: The same kinds of reaction shape rocks, air and the clouds between the stars.
explanations.description: Rain joins with carbon dioxide from the air and becomes a very weak acid. Over thousands of years this acid dissolves limestone and makes caves. Inside the cave, dripping water loses carbon dioxide, and solid limestone precipitates. It grows into stalactites, as in the Borra Caves in Andhra Pradesh. High above the Earth, sunlight splits oxygen molecules into single atoms. Each atom joins another oxygen molecule and makes ozone, which shields life from harsh sunlight. Astronomers have found more than 200 kinds of molecule in the clouds between the stars, including water. The Sun itself does not burn. Inside the Sun, the centres of atoms join. That is a nuclear reaction, and it changes the atoms themselves.
examples: Carbon dioxide + water → carbonic acid, in rain.
Sunlight splits oxygen high in the air, and the atoms join to make ozone.
Water and other molecules form on dust grains in clouds between the stars.
explanations.art: A cave with pointed stalactites hanging from the roof and a drop of water falling from the tip of one.

agreed.text: In every chemical reaction the atoms are kept. None is made and none is lost.
agreed.evidence: Antoine Lavoisier weighed reactions in sealed glass vessels in the 1770s and 1780s. The total weight was the same before and after. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier recorded and drew the experiments.

agreed.text: Burning is a reaction with oxygen. A burning thing takes something in from the air.
agreed.evidence: Metals such as tin and mercury become heavier when they are heated in air. Lavoisier showed that the extra weight equals the weight of the air that was used up.

agreed.text: Acid curdles milk by cancelling the charge on the casein clusters, so that they stick together.
agreed.evidence: Dairy scientists measure the charge on casein clusters as acid is added. The charge falls to zero at about pH 4.6, and the casein then comes out of the milk.

agreed.text: Substances react in fixed amounts, so a reaction stops when one reactant is used up.
agreed.evidence: The French chemist Joseph Proust analysed many compounds in the 1790s. Each compound always held the same elements in the same proportions by weight, however it was made.

agreed.text: Breaking bonds takes energy in, and making bonds gives energy out.
agreed.evidence: Chemists measure the heat of reactions in an insulated cup with a thermometer. Setting plaster warms the cup. Baking soda splits only while heat is supplied.

agreed.text: Many reactions can run in both directions. The amounts and the conditions decide which way they go.
agreed.evidence: Claude-Louis Berthollet saw a well-known swapping reaction running backwards at the salt lakes of Egypt in 1799. In 1864 Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage in Norway turned this into an exact rule.

challenging.claim: Burning is a splitting. A burning thing gives off a substance called phlogiston and leaves ash behind.
challenging.who: Georg Stahl, a German chemist, in about 1700, and most chemists for the next 70 years.
challenging.for: Wood turns into a small heap of light ash, so it seems to have lost something.
challenging.against: Metals get heavier when they burn. Lavoisier showed that burning things join with oxygen from the air. The gases that wood gives off were not being weighed.

challenging.claim: Each substance has fixed likes and dislikes, so a swapping reaction can go only one way.
challenging.who: Torbern Bergman, a Swedish chemist, in 1775.
challenging.for: In the laboratory, the same swap gave the same products every time.
challenging.against: Berthollet saw the same swap running backwards in Egypt, where one reactant was present in a huge amount. Amounts matter as well as likes.

challenging.claim: Milk that has curdled has always gone bad.
challenging.for: Milk left out for too long turns sour and lumpy, and it can make people ill.
challenging.against: Fresh hot milk curdled with lemon juice is paneer, and it is safe. Old milk curdles because bacteria have made acid in the milk. The curdling is the same reaction, but the source of the acid is different.

challenging.claim: If you keep adding one reactant, you keep getting more product.
challenging.for: Two lemons give more juice than one, so more lemon should give more curds.
challenging.against: The amount of product is set by the reactant that runs out first. Once the casein is used up, extra lemon juice only makes the whey more sour.

challenging.claim: Every reaction belongs to exactly one of the four kinds.
challenging.who: A simple reading of school books.
challenging.for: Most reactions that children meet fit one pattern well.
challenging.against: Burning hydrogen is also a joining. The fizz of vinegar and baking soda is a swap followed by a split. The kinds are a way of sorting that people made.

challenging.claim: Sorting reactions by pattern is less useful than sorting them by what moves between the substances.
challenging.for: Sorting by moving electrons or moving hydrogen explains why reactions happen, and covers reactions that fit no simple pattern.
challenging.against: The four patterns can be seen without knowing about electrons, and they help a learner guess the products. Both ways of sorting are in use.

big_questions.q: Milk turns into curds and whey. Is the milk gone, or is it still there in another form?
big_questions.hint: Every atom of the milk is still in the bowl, just joined in a new way. So what is it that has changed?

big_questions.q: Burning fits two kinds at once. So are the four kinds found in nature, or made by people?
big_questions.hint: Think of sorting clothes by colour or by owner. Is one way the true way?

big_questions.q: Gypsum can be split into plaster and joined into gypsum again and again. Can every reaction be undone?
big_questions.hint: Could you turn curds and whey back into milk? Could you turn smoke back into wood? A tree actually does something close to that, because it builds wood from the carbon dioxide in the air.

big_questions.q: Your body splits food and joins the pieces into you. Are you a thing, or reactions that keep going?
big_questions.hint: A candle flame keeps the same shape, yet the wax and the air going through it change every second. Are you a little like that flame?

big_questions.q: People burned seashells into lime for thousands of years before anyone knew about atoms. Did they understand the reaction?
big_questions.hint: They knew exactly what to do and what would happen. Is that the same as knowing why?

big_questions.q: Burning fuel cooks food and moves buses. It also changes everyone's air. Who should decide how much is burned?
big_questions.hint: The people who burn the most fuel are not always the people harmed most by the change in the air.

story.title: The Sack That Did Not Hiss
story.note: Thangam, her grandmother Ponni Aaya, the mason Murugesan and their village on the Tamil Nadu coast are made up. Aaya is a Tamil word for grandmother. These things are real. People on India's coasts have burned seashells in small kilns to make lime for plaster for a very long time. A kiln's heat splits the shell into quicklime and carbon dioxide gas. Quicklime joins with water, hisses, swells and gets very hot. Quicklime kept in damp air slowly joins with water, and then with carbon dioxide from the air. After that it no longer heats up in water. Lime plaster on a wall hardens over months and years. It takes in carbon dioxide and turns back into the substance of shell. Quicklime burns skin and eyes, so children must never handle it.
text: Six sacks of lime stood in Aaya's shed, and the mason's cart was already coming down the beach road.

Thangam was nine. Her grandmother, whom she called Aaya, burned seashells into lime, as her own mother had done. Every house in the village had been plastered with Aaya's lime. So had the old school, and the temple wall that faced the sea.
"Murugesan needs all six today," Aaya said. "The big house on the east street must be plastered before the wedding. Go and see that the sacks are tied."

Thangam knew how lime was made. She had helped to carry the clam shells up from the shore in baskets. She had watched Aaya pack the round kiln, one layer of shells and one layer of charcoal, up to the top. The kiln burned for a night and a day. The shells came out with the same shape, but they were white, light and easy to crumble. Aaya called them live lime. She never touched them with wet hands, and she tied a cloth over her nose when she filled the sacks.

Two of the sacks were from yesterday's burning. The other four were from the burning three weeks ago, before the rains came. It had rained every day since then, and the shed roof dripped in one corner. The air in the shed felt as wet as a towel.

One of the old sacks had split at the seam, and a few white lumps had rolled out. Thangam picked up a broken pot and put one lump in it. She liked this part. She stood back, as Aaya had taught her, and poured in half a coconut shell of water from the full length of her arm.
Nothing happened.
There was no hiss and no crack. No steam rose. The lump sat in the water like a stone from the road. Thangam waited, and then she touched the outside of the pot. It was cold.
She thought the water might be at fault, so she fetched more from the well. It made no difference.
Then she took a lump from one of yesterday's sacks, with the iron ladle and not with her fingers. She put it in a second pot and poured water from the same coconut shell.
The lump hissed at once. It cracked and swelled and fell apart, and steam rolled over the rim. When she held her palm near the pot, the heat pushed it away.
The two lumps had come from the same shells, the same kiln and the same water. One was alive, and one was not.
"Aaya!" she called. "The old lime has died."
Aaya came and looked into both pots. She did not seem surprised, and she did not explain. "Why do you think it died?" she asked.
Thangam looked at the dripping corner of the roof. She looked at the old sacks, which were damp and dark at the bottom.

"Live lime wants water," she said slowly. "When it gets water, it hisses and gets hot, and then it is finished. It can do that only once." She pressed her hand flat on an old sack. "These have been sitting in wet air for three weeks. They took the water out of the air, a little every day. They have already hissed, Aaya. They did it so slowly that nobody heard."

Aaya nodded. "And after the water, it takes something more from the air, a part of the air that you cannot see. Then it is on its way back to being shell. Half of that sack is shell dust now. If you plaster a wall with shell dust, the wall comes off on your hand."
The cart stopped outside. Murugesan the mason jumped down. He was a large, cheerful man, and he was in a hurry.
"Six sacks, Ponni Aaya. I have eight men waiting."
"Two sacks," said Thangam.
He laughed. "I can count six from here, little one."
"Four of them are dead," she said. "Watch." She set out two clean pots and put one old lump and one new lump in them. She gave him the coconut shell and made him stand back.
He poured water on the old lump, and nothing happened. He poured water on the new one and jumped away from the steam.

For a moment Murugesan said nothing. Then he said, "If I had put that on the wedding house, it would be dusting off the wall while the guests ate." He turned to her grandmother. "Who taught her to test it?"
"She asked the lime," said Aaya, "and the lime answered."
He took the two live sacks. He would come back for more in three days.
That evening Thangam helped to carry the four old sacks to the kiln. Aaya packed their dull lumps between layers of charcoal, just as she packed fresh shells.
"Will the fire bring them back?" Thangam asked.
"The fire will drive out the water and the unseen air. What is left will be live lime again. It has been round this road before."
Thangam went and stood by the wall of their own house. Aaya's mother had plastered it long before Thangam was born. She put her palm on it, and it was cool and hard.
Once it had been shells in the sea. The fire had made it into lime, and water had made it into paste. Then the air had come to it slowly, for years, and now it was almost shell again.
Behind her, Aaya lit the kiln.
story.epiphany: Thangam saw that live lime can join with water only once. The old sacks had slowly joined with water from the damp air. So nothing was left to react when she poured water on them. Heat could split them again and make them ready to join once more.
ask: Both lumps came from the same shells and the same kiln. Why did only one of them get hot in water?
The kiln's fire and the water did opposite things to the lime. Which one was a splitting and which was a joining?
Thangam tested a lump from each sack before the mason took them. What could you test before trusting an old packet of baking soda?

games.title: Join, Split, Swap or Burn: the reaction card game
games.context: This is a card game about the four kinds of reaction. Each card describes a real reaction in words. You decide if it is a joining, a splitting, a swapping or a burning.
