printables.title: 4 kind tokens: JOIN, SPLIT, SWAP, BURN. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player chooses one kind token and puts it face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the kind on the back scores 1 point.
Three cards have two kinds on the back. Either kind scores 1 point. A player who names both kinds aloud before the back is read scores 2 points.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read the front, say the kind aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right kind.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 24 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes a real reaction. Your four tokens are the four kinds: join, split, swap and burn. Count the substances before and after the reaction. That is the best clue.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Join, Split, Swap or Burn. You set up the reaction cards and the kind tokens.

flow.do: Play the first twelve cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card six.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a kind token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which kind the reaction is?
good: I counted the substances before and after.
Two became one, so it is a joining.
It had a fuel and oxygen, so it is burning.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask how many substances there are before the reaction and how many after. A child playing alone can do the same: say the kind aloud, and then check the back of the card.
flow.context: In this step of Join, Split, Swap or Burn you play the first twelve reaction cards.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Twelve more cards. Some reactions fit two kinds. If you think a card has two kinds, say both before I read the back.
flow.kid: Play twelve more cards. Some fit two kinds. Say both if you can.
flow.context: In this step of Join, Split, Swap or Burn you play the last twelve cards and look for two-kind reactions.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 24 cards into four heaps by kind. Put the three two-kind cards between their heaps.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into four heaps. Where should the rocket engine card go? Now look at the splitting heap. What do most of those reactions need to be given: heat, electricity or light?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into four heaps. Which cards sit between two heaps?

check.q: One substance goes in, and two substances come out. Which kind of reaction is it?
check.why: In a splitting reaction, one substance becomes two or more. If you chose joining, that is the reverse: two become one. In a swap there are two substances before and two after.

flow.context: This is the last step of Join, Split, Swap or Burn. You sort the 24 reaction cards into heaps by kind.

experiments.title: Second Squeeze: which ran out, the milk or the lemon?
experiments.question: Lemon juice turns hot milk into curds and whey. If more lemon juice is added to the whey, do more curds form? If fresh milk is added to the whey, do curds form?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will more lemon juice make new curds in the whey? Will a spoon of fresh milk make new curds in the whey? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers get whey from the same bowl, 5 tablespoons each, at the same warmth. Tumbler A gets only lemon juice. Tumbler B gets only hot milk. Stir each one the same way, 5 times round. Wait 1 minute before you decide. Only one thing differs between the tumblers: what was added.

materials.item: milk, 300 millilitres (one and a half tumblers)
lemons or limes, squeezed and strained, to give about 8 teaspoons of juice (or 8 teaspoons of white vinegar)
a small pan, and a steel bowl for making the curds
a tea strainer or a clean thin cotton cloth, and a second bowl to catch the whey
clear glass tumblers, marked A and B
a teaspoon, a tablespoon, and a notebook page with a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up heats the milk and pours everything that is hot. The child adds lemon juice and stirs with a long spoon. Keep hands away from the hot bowl.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three columns: the tumbler, what you added, and what you saw after 1 minute. Then write how many tablespoons of milk tumbler B took before the milk stayed white.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make curds from hot milk and lemon juice. Then you test the leftover whey, to find out which reactant was used up.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring steaming milk from a small pan into a steel bowl, with some milk kept back in the pan under a lid.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up heats 300 millilitres of milk. Pour 200 millilitres into a bowl. Keep the rest hot in the covered pan.

setup.art: A child adding a teaspoon of lemon juice to the bowl of hot milk and stirring, with white curds beginning to form.
setup.caption: 2. Add lemon juice, 1 teaspoon at a time. Stir and count the teaspoons until curds and clear whey appear.

setup.art: A tea strainer full of white curds held over a bowl of pale yellow-green whey.
setup.caption: 3. Strain out the curds. Put 5 tablespoons of warm whey into tumbler A and 5 into tumbler B.

setup.art: Two glass tumblers of pale whey marked A and B, with a teaspoon of lemon juice over A and a tablespoon of milk over B.
setup.caption: 4. Add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice to A. Add 1 tablespoon of hot milk to B. Watch for 1 minute.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: 4 tablespoons of hot milk, one at a time

flow.do: Squeeze and strain the lemons. Mark the tumblers A and B. Ask for both guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: We will turn milk into curds and whey with lemon juice. Then we will add more lemon to some whey, and fresh milk to some whey. Which one will make new curds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lemon makes curds in milk. Will more lemon make curds in whey? Will more milk? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think more lemon juice will or will not make new curds in the whey?
good: More lemon should make more curds.
The whey has no milk left in it.
The curds have already come out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect more lemon to make more curds. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Second Squeeze. You guess what lemon juice and fresh milk will each do to whey.

flow.do: Heat 300 millilitres of milk until it just starts to rise, then turn off the flame. Pour 200 millilitres into the steel bowl. Cover the pan to keep the rest hot. Your child adds lemon juice, 1 teaspoon at a time, and stirs gently for 10 seconds each time.
flow.say: Add one teaspoon of lemon juice and stir slowly. Tell me what you see. Count each teaspoon aloud. Stop when you see white lumps in a clear, pale liquid.
flow.kid: Add lemon juice, one teaspoon at a time. Stir slowly. Count the teaspoons until curds appear.
flow.parent: Most milk needs 2 to 4 teaspoons. The first teaspoon often seems to do nothing. When the whey turns clear and pale yellow-green, add 1 more teaspoon and stop. Write down the total.
flow.context: In this step of Second Squeeze you add lemon juice to hot milk until curds and whey form.

flow.do: Pour the bowl through the strainer into the second bowl. Keep the curds aside. Measure 5 tablespoons of the warm whey into tumbler A and 5 into tumbler B.
flow.say: The solid in the strainer is called curds. The thin liquid is called whey. Look at the whey closely. Do you see any milk left in it?
flow.kid: Strain out the curds. Put 5 tablespoons of whey in A. Put 5 in B.
flow.parent: Do the next step straight away, while the whey is still warm. Cold whey curdles new milk slowly and only a little.
flow.context: In this step of Second Squeeze you strain out the curds and put warm whey in tumblers A and B.

flow.do: Add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice to tumbler A. Add 1 tablespoon of hot milk from the pan to tumbler B. Stir each 5 times. Watch both for 1 minute against the light, and write what you see.
flow.say: Tumbler A gets more lemon juice. Tumbler B gets fresh milk. Stir both, and watch for one minute. In which tumbler do new curds appear?
flow.kid: Add lemon to A. Add milk to B. Stir. Which one makes new curds?

check.q: In Second Squeeze, why do both tumblers get whey from the same bowl?
options: So only the added thing differs
So there is less washing up
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing differs. Both tumblers hold the same whey, so any difference comes from what was added. If you chose washing up or heat, think about what you want to compare.

flow.parent: Tumbler A usually stays clear. Tumbler B usually shows white flecks or soft lumps within a minute. If B only turns cloudy, the whey has cooled. Stand the tumbler in a bowl of hot water for 2 minutes.
flow.context: In this step of Second Squeeze you add lemon juice to tumbler A and hot milk to tumbler B.

flow.do: Keep adding hot milk to tumbler B, 1 tablespoon at a time. Stir, wait half a minute, and look for new curds. Count the tablespoons. Stop when the new milk stays white and makes no curds. Then add 1 teaspoon of lemon juice to B.
flow.say: Add another tablespoon of milk to B and look for new curds. Keep count. Tell me when the milk stays white. Now add one teaspoon of lemon juice. What happens?
flow.kid: Add milk to B, one tablespoon at a time. Count. Stop when the milk stays white.
flow.parent: The milk usually stays white after 2 to 6 tablespoons in all. If curds still form when the milk in the pan is finished, write that down as your result. The last teaspoon of lemon juice should bring curds back.
flow.context: In this step of Second Squeeze you keep adding hot milk to tumbler B until no new curds form.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. In the first bowl, which ran out, the milk or the lemon? In tumbler B at the end, which ran out?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did more lemon juice make no new curds in tumbler A?
good: The part of the milk that makes curds was used up.
All the casein had already come out as curds.
The lemon had nothing left to work on.

ask.q: Why did tumbler B stop making curds after a few spoons of milk?
good: The leftover acid in the whey was used up.
Each spoon of milk used some of the acid.
This time the lemon ran out, and not the milk.

flow.parent: The reason: curds are made from casein, the main milk protein, and the acid in lemon juice. In the first bowl, all the casein became curds, and some acid was left in the whey. So more lemon did nothing in A, and fresh milk made curds in B. Each spoon of milk used up some of the leftover acid. When the acid was gone, the milk stayed white. A reaction stops when one reactant is used up. Use the curds as paneer, and use the whey from the first bowl in dal or dough.
flow.think: A cook has curdled a pot of milk, but the whey still looks milky. Should she add more milk or more lemon juice?
flow.context: This is the last step of Second Squeeze. You say which reactant was used up in the bowl and in tumbler B.

experiments.title: Powder and Water: which powder joins with the water?
experiments.question: Plaster of Paris and fine sand are each mixed with water. Does either one get warm? Does either one go hard while it is still wet? What happens to each lump in water the next day?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will either cup get warm? Which paste will go hard first, and will it be hard before it is dry? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two paper cups of the same size. Put 6 level tablespoons of powder and 3 tablespoons of water in each. Use water from the same tumbler. Stir each one 20 times. Keep the cups side by side, away from the sun and the fan. Touch and poke both cups at the same times. Only the powder differs.

materials.item: plaster of Paris, 6 level tablespoons
fine dry sand, 6 level tablespoons (or stone kolam powder, or two sticks of chalk crushed to powder)
paper cups, marked A and B
ice cream sticks or old spoons for stirring, and toothpicks for poking
a tablespoon, a tumbler of water, and a clock or phone timer
a bowl of water for the next day, and old newspaper to work on

experiments.safety: A grown-up measures and mixes the plaster. Do not breathe in the dust, and keep it away from eyes. Never put a finger or a hand into setting plaster, because it gets hot and grips the skin. Throw leftover plaster in the dustbin and never down a sink.

schedule.what: Mix the two cups, then touch and poke them every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.
Tear off the cups, put both lumps in water for 5 minutes, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes. For each cup write warm or not warm, and soft or hard. On day 2, write what each lump did in water.
experiments.context: In this two-day experiment you mix plaster of Paris with water, and sand with water. You find out which powder joins with the water to make a new solid.

setup.art: Two paper cups marked A and B on newspaper, with a bag of white plaster powder beside A and a small heap of sand beside B.
setup.caption: 1. Put 6 level tablespoons of plaster in cup A. Put 6 level tablespoons of sand in cup B.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring white paste in cup A with an ice cream stick, while a child watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Add 3 tablespoons of water to each cup. Stir each one 20 times. Start the timer.

setup.art: A child's palm resting on the outside of cup A, and a toothpick standing upright in the paste.
setup.caption: 3. Every 5 minutes, touch the outside of each cup and poke the top with a toothpick.

setup.art: A hard white lump and a crumbling heap of wet sand sitting in a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 4. Next day, tear off the cups. Put both lumps in water for 5 minutes.

flow.do: Spread newspaper. Mark the cups A and B. Show your child the two dry powders. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will mix each powder with the same amount of water. Will either cup get warm? Which will go hard first? Will it be hard before it is dry? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the two powders. Which will go hard with water? Will a cup get warm? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a paste goes hard?
good: The water dries away.
The powder sticks together.
The powder and the water make something new.

flow.parent: Most children say that things go hard by drying. Do not correct this. The test will check it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Powder and Water. You guess what plaster and sand will each do when mixed with water.

flow.do: Put 6 level tablespoons of plaster in cup A and 6 of sand in cup B. Add 3 tablespoons of water to each. Stir each one 20 times. Start the timer.
flow.say: I will mix the plaster, because the dust must not be breathed in. You stir the sand. Both cups get the same water and the same stirring.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes the plaster. You stir the sand 20 times. Start the timer.
flow.parent: The plaster should look like thick curd. If it is too stiff to stir, add 1 more tablespoon of water to both cups.
flow.context: In this step of Powder and Water you mix 6 tablespoons of each powder with 3 tablespoons of water.

flow.do: At 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes, your child holds a palm on the outside of each cup. Then they poke the top of each paste with a toothpick. Write warm or not warm, and soft or hard.
flow.say: Hold each cup for a slow count of five. Is one warmer? Now poke each one gently. Is the top wet? Is it hard? Tell me, and I will write it down.
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, hold each cup. Poke each top. Say warm or not, soft or hard.

check.q: In Powder and Water, the plaster goes hard while its top is still wet. What does that show?
options: It did not harden by drying
check.why: A thing that hardens by drying must lose its water first. The plaster was hard and still wet, so the water was still inside. If you chose drying or leaking, look again: the cup is not dry and nothing ran out.

flow.parent: Cup A usually thickens in 5 to 10 minutes and feels warm between 10 and 20 minutes. The warmth is gentle with this amount, so compare the two cups with the same hand. Cup B stays cool and soft.
flow.context: In this step of Powder and Water you touch and poke both cups every 5 minutes.

flow.do: Leave both cups on a shelf until the next day. Ask the question below before you leave them.
flow.say: By tomorrow both cups will be dry. We will put both lumps in a bowl of water. What do you think each lump will do?
flow.kid: Leave the cups until tomorrow. What will each lump do in water?
flow.wait: Leave both cups until the next day
flow.context: In this step of Powder and Water you leave the plaster cup and the sand cup until the next day.

flow.do: Day 2. Tear the paper cups away. Put both lumps in a bowl of water for 5 minutes. Then your child presses each lump with a thumb.
flow.say: Both lumps are dry now. Put them in the water and wait five minutes. Now press each one. Which one is still a solid block?
flow.kid: Tear off the cups. Put both lumps in water. Wait 5 minutes. Press each one.
flow.parent: The plaster stays a hard block. The sand lump falls apart, or turns back into wet sand. Chalk powder turns into a soft paste.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Powder and Water. You put the dry plaster lump and the dry sand lump in water.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Where is the water that we put into the plaster cup?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What three things show that the plaster and the water made a new substance?
good: The cup got warm.
It went hard while it was still wet.
The lump stayed hard in water the next day.

ask.q: Where did the water in cup B go?
good: It dried into the air.
The sand is the same sand as before, so the water just dried away.

flow.parent: The reason: plaster of Paris joins with water. The two become one new solid called gypsum, and the water is locked inside it. Making the new bonds gives out heat, so the cup felt warm. This is a joining reaction. Sand does not react with water. The water only dried away, and the same sand was left. Stick chalk is often made of gypsum, so it is plaster that has already joined with water.
flow.think: A doctor wraps a wet plaster bandage round a broken arm. Why does the cast feel warm for a few minutes?
flow.context: This is the last step of Powder and Water. You say what the warmth, the hardening and the water test show.

experiments.title: Soap and Sour: what does vinegar do to soap?
experiments.question: Soap water makes foam when it is shaken. If vinegar is added, does the soap water still foam? Does dish wash liquid behave in the same way?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which bottle will have the tallest foam, and which the shortest? Will the liquid in any bottle change how it looks? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three clear bottles of the same size. Put 4 tablespoons of liquid in each. Add 2 teaspoons of water or vinegar to each. Shake every bottle 10 times, in the same way. Measure the foam at once with a ruler. Do the whole test twice. Bottles A and B differ only in what was added. Bottles B and C differ only in the kind of cleaner.

materials.item: a bar of bath soap (the wrapper should say 'soap'), grated to give 1 level teaspoon
dish wash liquid or shampoo, 3 drops
white vinegar, 4 teaspoons (or strained lemon juice)
small clear bottles with lids, marked A, B and C
a tumbler of warm drinking water (200 millilitres), and a tumbler of plain water
a teaspoon, a tablespoon, a ruler and a notebook page

experiments.safety: Keep soap water and vinegar away from eyes. Do not taste anything in this test. A grown-up grates the soap.
experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for each bottle. Write the foam height for try 1 and try 2. Write how the liquid looks: clear, cloudy or milky, with or without white bits.
experiments.context: In this experiment you shake soap water with plain water and with vinegar, and measure the foam. You also test dish wash liquid with vinegar.

setup.art: A grown-up grating a bar of soap into a tumbler of warm water, with a child stirring.
setup.caption: 1. Stir 1 level teaspoon of grated soap into 200 millilitres of warm water until it dissolves.

setup.art: Three small clear bottles marked A, B and C, each with a little liquid in the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Put 4 tablespoons of soap water in A and in B. Put 4 tablespoons of water and 3 drops of dish wash liquid in C.

setup.art: A teaspoon of plain water held over bottle A and a teaspoon of vinegar held over bottle B.
setup.caption: 3. Add 2 teaspoons of water to A. Add 2 teaspoons of vinegar to B and to C.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler against a bottle with a tall layer of white foam, beside a bottle of milky liquid with almost no foam.
setup.caption: 4. Shake each bottle 10 times. Measure the foam at once. Look at the liquid.

flow.do: Set out the three bottles, the soap and the vinegar. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Bottle A will hold soap water and plain water. Bottle B will hold soap water and vinegar. Bottle C will hold dish wash liquid and vinegar. Which will foam most when we shake it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three bottles. Each holds soap or dish wash, with water or vinegar. Which will foam most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think vinegar will or will not change the foam?
good: Vinegar is sour and soap is soapy, so they may react.
Vinegar is mostly water, so nothing will change.
Lemon takes the soapy feel off my hands.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soap and Sour. You guess which of three bottles will foam most.

flow.do: Grate the soap. Stir 1 level teaspoon into 200 millilitres of warm water until no bits are left. Put 4 tablespoons into bottle A and 4 into bottle B. Put 4 tablespoons of plain water and 3 drops of dish wash liquid into bottle C.
flow.say: Stir until the soap has dissolved. Now measure four tablespoons into A and four into B. Bottle C gets plain water and three drops of dish wash liquid.
flow.kid: Stir the soap into warm water. Fill A and B. Put water and dish wash in C.
flow.parent: Soap water is a little cloudy, and that is fine. If your tap water is hard, use filtered or boiled water, because hard water also reacts with soap.
flow.context: In this step of Soap and Sour you make soap water and fill bottles A, B and C.

flow.do: Add 2 teaspoons of plain water to A. Add 2 teaspoons of vinegar to B and 2 to C. Close the lids. Your child shakes each bottle 10 times and measures the foam at once. Write the heights and how each liquid looks.
flow.say: Add the water to A and the vinegar to B and C. Look at bottle B before you shake it. What do you see? Now shake each bottle ten times and measure the foam.
flow.kid: Add water to A. Add vinegar to B and C. Shake each 10 times. Measure the foam.

check.q: In Soap and Sour, why does bottle A get 2 teaspoons of plain water?
options: So every bottle holds the same amount
check.why: Bottle B gets 2 teaspoons of vinegar. Bottle A gets the same amount of plain water, so that only the vinegar differs. If you chose cleaner soap or taller foam, remember that a fair test changes one thing.

flow.parent: Bottle B usually turns milky white as soon as the vinegar goes in, and makes little or no foam. Bottle A foams well. Bottle C stays clear and still foams.
flow.context: In this step of Soap and Sour you add water or vinegar, shake each bottle and measure the foam.

flow.do: Empty and rinse the bottles, and do the whole test once more. Then leave bottle B to stand for 5 minutes and look at the top of the liquid.
flow.say: We do the test twice, because one try can be a fluke. Now let bottle B stand. Look at the top of the liquid. What has collected there?
flow.kid: Do the test once more. Then let B stand. What floats on top?
flow.parent: White, greasy bits usually float to the top of bottle B. Let your child rub one between two fingers. It feels waxy, and it does not foam.
flow.context: In this step of Soap and Sour you repeat the test and look at what floats in bottle B.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Is the white solid in bottle B still soap?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What shows that the white bits in bottle B are a new substance and not soap?
good: They do not dissolve in the water.
They do not make foam.
They feel waxy, not slippery.

ask.q: Why did the dish wash liquid still foam with vinegar?
good: It is a different substance from soap.
It does not make a solid with vinegar.

flow.parent: The reason: soap has a long fatty part joined to sodium. Vinegar is an acid, and it has hydrogen to give. The sodium and the hydrogen swap places. The fatty part with hydrogen is a waxy solid that does not dissolve, so it shows as white bits. A solid that forms like this is called a precipitate. The sodium stays dissolved as a salt. This is a swapping reaction. Dish wash liquid is made of other substances, which stay dissolved in sour water and in hard water.
flow.think: Soap leaves a grey ring on a bucket in homes with hard water. What might be happening to the soap?
flow.context: This is the last step of Soap and Sour. You say what the foam heights and the white bits show.

activities.title: The Pan and the Lid: can heat split a powder?

materials.item: cooking soda, also called baking soda, 2 heaped teaspoons (baking powder is a different thing)
a small dry steel or aluminium pan
cold, dry steel plates or lids that cover the pan
a dry spoon for stirring, and a cloth or tongs for lifting the lid

schedule.what: Heat baking soda under a cold lid, look for water drops, then test the same powder again.

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the heating and lifts the hot lids. The heated powder is washing soda, which stings eyes and skin. Do not taste it, and wash hands after the activity.
activities.record: Draw three lids: from the empty pan, from the first heating and from the second heating. Draw the drops on each one.
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up heats dry baking soda in a pan under a cold steel lid. You look for water drops on the lid, to find out if heat splits the powder.

setup.art: An empty small steel pan on a low gas flame, covered with a steel plate, with a grown-up's hand holding a cloth near the lid.
setup.caption: 1. Heat the empty dry pan under a cold lid for 1 minute. Look under the lid.

setup.art: Two heaped teaspoons of white powder in the pan, with a second cold steel plate about to cover it.
setup.caption: 2. Put in 2 heaped teaspoons of baking soda. Cover with a new cold lid for 1 minute.

setup.art: The underside of a steel lid covered in small drops of water, held up by a grown-up for a child to see.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the lid. Look for water drops underneath.

setup.art: The same pan of white powder covered again with a third dry steel plate.
setup.caption: 4. Stir and heat for 5 more minutes. Then cover with a third cold, dry lid for 1 minute.

flow.do: Show your child the dry baking soda and the dry pan. Rub a little powder between your fingers to show it is dry. Ask the question below and write down the answer.
flow.say: This powder is dry, and the pan is dry. I will heat the powder under a cold lid. What do you think we will find under the lid? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The powder is dry. A grown-up heats it under a lid. What will be under the lid? Why?

ask.q: Could anything come out of a dry powder when it is heated?
good: No, because it is dry.
Maybe smoke.
Maybe a gas, because baking soda makes cakes rise.

flow.parent: Most children expect nothing, or smoke. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Pan and the Lid. You guess what heat will do to dry baking soda.

flow.do: Heat the empty dry pan on a low flame under the first cold lid for 1 minute. Lift the lid with a cloth and show the underside. Take the pan off the flame.
flow.say: First we heat the pan with nothing in it. Look under the lid. Is it wet or dry? We need this, so we know what an empty pan does.
flow.kid: First the empty pan is heated. Look under the lid. Is it wet or dry?
flow.parent: The lid should be dry. This is the comparison for the next step.
flow.context: In this step of The Pan and the Lid the empty pan is heated under a cold lid.

flow.do: Put 2 heaped teaspoons of baking soda in the pan. Cover it with the second cold lid. Heat on a low flame for 1 minute. Lift the lid with a cloth and show the underside.
flow.say: Now the powder goes in. I will heat it for one minute under a new cold lid. Look under the lid now. What do you see? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: Now the powder is heated. Look under the lid. What do you see?

ask.q: The powder was dry. So where did the drops come from?
good: Out of the powder.
The heat pushed water out of the baking soda.
The powder had water joined inside it.

flow.parent: A mist of small water drops usually covers the lid. A cold lid works best. If you see no drops, heat for 1 more minute.
flow.context: In this step of The Pan and the Lid baking soda is heated under a cold lid for 1 minute.

flow.do: Heat the powder without a lid for 5 more minutes, stirring now and then. Watch the powder as you stir. Then cover the pan with the third cold, dry lid for 1 minute. Lift the lid and look.
flow.say: Watch the powder while I stir. Does it move like a dry powder? Now I cover it with a new dry lid. Do you think drops will come again? Why?
flow.kid: Watch the powder as it is stirred. Then a new lid goes on. Will drops come again?

check.q: In The Pan and the Lid, heated baking soda makes water drops once and not the second time. Why?
options: The baking soda was used up
check.why: Heat split all the baking soda in the first heating, so none was left to split. If you chose the lid or the flame, remember that the lid was cold and the flame was the same.

flow.parent: While it splits, the powder shifts and bubbles gently, almost like a liquid, because gas is leaving it. The third lid should stay dry, or show very few drops.
flow.context: In this step of The Pan and the Lid the same powder is heated a second time.

flow.do: Let the pan cool fully. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Is the powder in the pan still baking soda?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: The reason: heat splits baking soda into three substances. They are washing soda, water and carbon dioxide gas. The water left as steam and turned to drops on the cold lid. The gas left unseen, and made the powder bubble. The powder left in the pan is washing soda. This is a splitting reaction, and it needs heat. The same splitting makes a cake rise in the oven. Keep the washing soda for cleaning greasy vessels, or wash it away with plenty of water.
flow.think: A cake batter with baking soda rises in the oven. Which of the three products lifts the cake?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Pan and the Lid. You say what the water drops on the lid show about heated baking soda.

activities.title: Will It Burn? Seven things in a candle flame

materials.item: a candle fixed on a steel plate, and a matchbox
steel tongs, and a steel spoon
a strip of newspaper as long as a finger, and a dry leaf (a dry curry leaf or bay leaf will do)
a small stone or a piece of broken clay pot, a pinch of salt, a pinch of ash from an incense stick, and a few drops of water
a bowl of water kept beside the plate

schedule.what: Guess which of seven things will burn, then watch a grown-up hold each one in a candle flame.

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the candle and holds every item in the flame with tongs. Tie back long hair and keep loose sleeves away. Drop anything that burns into the bowl of water. Do this near an open window.
activities.record: Draw a table with three columns: the thing, your guess, and what happened. Use the words 'burned' and 'did not burn'.
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up holds seven things in a candle flame, one at a time. You guess which will burn, and look for what the burning things share.

setup.art: Seven small things in a row on a steel plate: a paper strip, a dry leaf, a stone, a steel spoon, a pinch of salt, a pinch of grey ash and a few drops of water.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the seven things. Guess for each one: will it burn?

setup.art: A grown-up holding a strip of paper in a candle flame with steel tongs, over a steel plate, with a bowl of water beside it.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up holds each thing in the flame for 10 seconds, with tongs.

setup.art: A notebook table with seven rows and ticks or crosses in a column headed 'burned?'.
setup.caption: 3. Write what happened. Sort the things into 'burned' and 'did not burn'.

flow.do: Lay out the seven things: paper, dry leaf, stone, steel spoon, salt, ash and water. Your child writes a guess for each one. Ask for the reason.
flow.say: I will hold each of these in a candle flame for ten seconds. Which ones will burn? What do you think the burning ones have in common? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the seven things. Guess which ones will burn. Why those?

ask.q: What do you think makes a thing able to burn?
good: It is dry.
It came from a plant.
It is thin and light.

flow.parent: Children often say that dry things burn. Salt, ash and stone are dry too, so the test will check that idea.
flow.context: This is the first step of Will It Burn. You guess which of seven things will burn in a candle flame.

flow.do: Light the candle. With tongs, hold each thing in the flame for 10 seconds. Hold the salt, the ash and the water in the steel spoon. Drop anything burning into the bowl of water.
flow.say: Watch each one closely. Does it catch fire and keep burning on its own? Or does it only get hot? Tell me what you see.
flow.kid: Watch each thing in the flame. Does it burn by itself? Or only get hot?
flow.parent: The paper and the leaf burn. The stone, the spoon, the salt and the ash do not. The water boils away. Salt turns the flame yellow, but the salt itself does not burn. The spoon gets a black coat of soot, which comes from the candle.
flow.context: In this step of Will It Burn a grown-up holds each of the seven things in the candle flame.

flow.do: Blow out the candle. Sort the seven things into two groups. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. What do the paper and the leaf share that the others lack?
flow.kid: Sort the things into two groups. What do the burning ones share?

check.q: Why does ash not burn in a candle flame?
options: Its atoms have already joined with oxygen
check.why: Burning is a fuel reacting with oxygen. Ash is what is left after that reaction, so it has nothing more to give. If you chose dry or small, remember that dry paper and small leaves burn well.

flow.parent: The reason: burning is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen. Paper and leaves were made by plants. They are built from carbon and hydrogen, which join with oxygen and give out heat. Water is hydrogen that has already joined with oxygen. Stone and ash are also joined with oxygen already. Salt is sodium joined with chlorine. A thick steel spoon carries the heat away. Very fine steel wool can burn.
flow.think: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, and hydrogen burns very well. So why does water put a fire out?
flow.context: This is the last step of Will It Burn. You sort the seven things and say what the burning ones share.

activities.title: Four Plates: build one reaction of each kind

materials.item: rajma beans, to be carbon atoms
white chana, to be oxygen atoms
green moong, to be hydrogen atoms
a groundnut to be a sodium atom, and a peppercorn to be a chlorine atom
steel plates, and a notebook page

schedule.what: Build four reactions from seeds, one on each plate, and count the atoms before and after.

activities.record: For each plate, write the word equation. Then write how many atoms of each kind there were before and after.
activities.context: In this activity seeds stand for atoms. You build one joining, one splitting, one swapping and one burning reaction, and count the atoms before and after each.

setup.art: Four small heaps on a table: red rajma beans, white chana, green moong and one groundnut with one peppercorn, each heap with a paper label.
setup.caption: 1. Rajma is carbon. Chana is oxygen. Moong is hydrogen. The groundnut is sodium. The peppercorn is chlorine.

setup.art: A steel plate with a line of chalk down the middle, seeds grouped as molecules on the left half and the right half empty.
setup.caption: 2. Build the reactants on the left half of the plate. Seeds that touch are joined by a bond.

setup.art: The same plate with the seeds moved to the right half in new groups.
setup.caption: 3. Move the same seeds to the right half and build the products. Count the seeds.

flow.do: Set out the seeds and say which atom each one stands for. Show that seeds placed touching each other are joined by bonds, and make one molecule.
flow.say: Each seed is one atom. Seeds that touch are joined by bonds, and together they are one molecule. One chana touching two moong is a water molecule. Build one for me.
flow.kid: Each seed is an atom. Touching seeds are joined. Build one water molecule.
flow.parent: Water is one oxygen and two hydrogens. Check that your child puts the chana in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Plates. You learn which seed stands for which atom, and build a water molecule.

flow.do: Plate 1, joining. Build carbon dioxide: 1 rajma touching 2 chana. Build water beside it. Then push all six seeds into one group, with the rajma in the middle. Plate 2, splitting. Build that same group of six, and pull it apart into water and carbon dioxide.
flow.say: On plate one, carbon dioxide and water join into carbonic acid, which is in soda. How many molecules before? How many after? On plate two, do the reverse.
flow.kid: Plate 1: push two molecules into one. Plate 2: pull one molecule into two.

ask.q: In the joining, did the number of atoms change? Did the number of molecules change?
good: The atoms stayed at six.
The molecules went from two to one.
Nothing was added or lost.

flow.parent: Carbonic acid is 1 carbon, 3 oxygens and 2 hydrogens. It splits again when soda goes flat.
flow.context: In this step of Four Plates you build a joining on plate 1 and a splitting on plate 2.

flow.do: Plate 3, swapping. Build an acid: 1 moong touching the peppercorn. Build a base: the groundnut touching 1 chana, which touches 1 moong. Now let the moong of the acid and the groundnut change places.
flow.say: This acid is hydrogen joined to chlorine. A base is the opposite of an acid, and it can cancel an acid. This base is sodium joined to oxygen and hydrogen. Swap the acid's hydrogen with the sodium. What two things have you made?
flow.kid: Plate 3: build the acid and the base. Swap the moong and the groundnut. What did you make?

ask.q: What are the two products on plate 3?
good: Groundnut with peppercorn, which is sodium with chlorine. That is salt.
A chana with two moong. That is water.

flow.parent: The products are table salt and water. This is the reaction between stomach acid and one kind of antacid.
flow.context: In this step of Four Plates you build a swapping reaction between an acid and a base on plate 3.

flow.do: Plate 4, burning. Build methane, the gas in piped cooking gas: 1 rajma touching 4 moong. Build 2 oxygen molecules: 2 chana touching, twice. Rearrange them into 1 carbon dioxide and 2 waters. Count the atoms before and after.
flow.say: Methane is the fuel. It burns with two oxygen molecules. Take everything apart and build carbon dioxide and water. Did the methane split? Did anything join with oxygen?
flow.kid: Plate 4: build methane and two oxygens. Rebuild them as carbon dioxide and two waters.

check.q: On the burning plate of Four Plates, 9 seeds are used before the reaction. How many after?
check.why: A reaction keeps every atom, so 9 seeds before means 9 seeds after. If you chose 3, you counted molecules. If you chose 12, check that no seed was added.

flow.parent: Before: 1 carbon, 4 hydrogens and 4 oxygens. After: the same 9 atoms. The methane came apart, and its atoms joined with oxygen. So this one burning reaction is a splitting and a joining at the same time.
flow.think: On every plate you broke some bonds and made new ones. Was there any plate where you only did one of these?
flow.context: This is the last step of Four Plates. You build the burning of methane on plate 4 and count the atoms.

projects.title: The Home Reaction Hunt: twelve reactions in two days

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a large sheet of paper or the back of an old calendar, for the chart
sketch pens in four colours

projects.safety: Only look at stoves, cleaners and medicines. Do not open or touch bottles of toilet cleaner or bleach. A grown-up walks round with the child.

schedule.what: Walk round your home with a grown-up and list twelve chemical reactions.
Sort the twelve reactions into the four kinds and make a chart.

projects.record: A chart with four columns: joining, splitting, swapping and burning. Write each reaction in its column, with the room where you found it.
projects.context: In this two-day project you hunt for twelve chemical reactions in your own home. Then you sort them into joining, splitting, swapping and burning.

setup.art: A child with a notebook standing at a kitchen door, looking at a gas stove, a pot of curd and a rusty window grill.
setup.caption: 1. Walk through the kitchen, the bathroom and the balcony. List twelve reactions.

setup.art: A notebook list with twelve lines such as 'gas stove flame', 'curd setting', 'rust on the grill' and 'grey ring on the bucket'.
setup.caption: 2. For each one, write the reactants and the products if you know them.

setup.art: A large chart with four coloured columns headed joining, splitting, swapping and burning, with reactions written under each.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, sort the twelve into four columns. Which column is longest?

flow.do: Day 1. Walk through the kitchen, the bathroom and the balcony with your child. Look for places where a new substance is being made. Your child lists twelve, with the room.
flow.say: A reaction makes a new substance. Where in our home is that happening now, or happening every day? Look for flames, rust, fizz, things setting and things going sour.
flow.kid: Walk round your home with a grown-up. Find twelve places where new substances are made.

ask.q: How can you tell that a new substance is being made?
good: There is a flame or heat.
The colour or smell changes for good.
A solid or a gas appears.

flow.parent: Ideas if your child is stuck. In the kitchen: the gas flame, milk setting into curd, idli batter rising, a cake rising, a cut apple turning brown. In the bathroom: a grey soap ring on a bucket, lemon on a soapy hand, an antacid tablet. Elsewhere: an incense stick, rust on a grill, a dark brass lamp, cement or wall putty setting.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Home Reaction Hunt. You list twelve chemical reactions that happen in your home.

flow.do: Day 2. Draw four columns on the large sheet. Your child writes each of the twelve reactions in a column. If one fits two columns, write it on the line between them.
flow.say: For each reaction, ask how many substances there are before and after. Two into one is joining. One into two is splitting. A fuel with oxygen is burning. An exchange is swapping.
flow.kid: Draw four columns. Put each reaction in its column. Some may fit two.
flow.parent: Guide, with answers: rust and tarnish are joining. Setting cement is joining. A rising cake is splitting. Rising idli batter is splitting, done by living yeasts and bacteria. Soap rings, antacids and curd are swapping. Flames and incense are burning. A browning apple is joining with oxygen.
flow.context: This is day 2 of The Home Reaction Hunt. You sort your twelve reactions into the four kinds on a chart.

flow.do: Count each column. Talk about the questions below. Put the chart on a wall.
flow.say: Which kind did you find most often? Which was hardest to find? Which reactions were done by living beings, such as bacteria?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which kind won? Which reactions did living beings do?

ask.q: Which reactions in your list were hard to sort, and why?
good: Burning also looked like joining.
I did not know the products.
Curd is made by bacteria and by acid.

flow.parent: There is no single right chart. A clear reason for each choice matters more than the column.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Home Reaction Hunt. You count which kind of reaction is most common in your home.

challenges.title: The Sharpest Coin Print: find the best plaster mix
challenges.problem: Plaster of Paris joins with water and sets hard. With too much water the print is weak and blurred. With too little, the paste sets before it takes the shape. Find the mix that copies a coin most sharply.
constraints: Use 2 level tablespoons of plaster for every mix.
Change only the amount of water.
Press the same kind of coin, the same way, into every mix.
Lift the coins after 20 minutes, and judge every print in the same way.
A grown-up mixes the plaster. No finger goes into wet plaster.
materials: 3 bottle caps or small paper cups, marked 1, 2 and 3
3 coins of the same kind with clear writing, and a drop of cooking oil to rub on them
a teaspoon, a tablespoon, water and an ice cream stick
old newspaper to work on, and a phone timer
general: Mix 2 tablespoons of plaster with 1 tablespoon of water. This is the usual mix, like thick curd.
Rub oil on each coin so that it lifts off cleanly.
Press a coin in gently after 1 minute, and leave it still.
creative: Tap the cup on the table ten times before pressing, to bring air bubbles to the top.
Sprinkle the powder on to the water and let it sink before stirring, as plaster workers do.
Press a leaf, a shell or a key in place of the coin, and compare the fine lines.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own best print. Choose the amount of water from your results, and add one idea of your own. Say why you think it will give a sharper print.
challenges.context: In this challenge you make three plaster mixes with different amounts of water. You press a coin into each one and find which mix gives the sharpest print.

setup.art: Three small paper cups marked 1, 2 and 3, each with white plaster paste of a different thickness, from runny to stiff.
setup.caption: 1. Make three mixes. Each has 2 tablespoons of plaster. The water is 2 tablespoons, 1 tablespoon and half a tablespoon.

setup.art: A child pressing an oiled coin face down into the paste in the middle cup.
setup.caption: 2. After 1 minute, press one oiled coin gently into each mix.

setup.art: Three hardened white discs side by side, each with a round coin print, the middle one showing the clearest letters.
setup.caption: 3. After 20 minutes, lift the coins. Which print can you read best?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Mark the cups 1, 2 and 3. Rub a drop of oil on each of the 3 coins. Ask which mix your child expects to win, and why.
flow.say: Cup one gets two tablespoons of water. Cup two gets one. Cup three gets half. Which will copy the coin best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three mixes: runny, medium and stiff. Which will copy the coin best? Why?

ask.q: What might go wrong with too much water, or with too little?
good: Too much water may stay soft.
Too little may set before the coin goes in.
A stiff paste may not fill the small letters.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Sharpest Coin Print. You guess which plaster mix will copy the coin best.

flow.do: Put 2 level tablespoons of plaster in each cup. Add 2 tablespoons of water to cup 1, 1 tablespoon to cup 2 and half a tablespoon to cup 3. Stir each 20 times. After 1 minute, your child presses one oiled coin into each.
flow.say: I will mix, and you will press the coins. Press each one gently until it is level with the top. Then leave it and do not move it.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes. You press one oiled coin gently into each cup.
flow.parent: Press the coin into cup 3 first, because the stiff mix sets soonest. Use three coins of the same kind, such as three 2-rupee coins.
flow.context: In this step of The Sharpest Coin Print you make the three mixes and press a coin into each.

flow.do: Wait 20 minutes. Your child touches the outside of each cup now and then. Then lift the coins, tip out each disc and compare the prints. Try to read the year. Scratch the back of each disc with a fingernail.
flow.say: Which cup feels warmest? Now look at the three prints. In which one is the writing clearest? Which disc is hardest to scratch?
flow.kid: Wait 20 minutes. Compare the three prints. Which can you read? Which is hardest?

check.q: A plaster mix has too much water. What happens to the extra water?
options: It is left over and weakens the cast
check.why: Plaster joins with a fixed amount of water. Extra water is left over between the crystals, and it leaves holes when it dries. If you chose more plaster or a harder cast, remember that a reaction stops when one reactant is used up.

flow.parent: The middle mix usually gives the sharpest and hardest print. The runny mix is slow, soft and chalky. The stiff mix is lumpy, with gaps.
flow.context: In this step of The Sharpest Coin Print you compare the three coin prints after 20 minutes.

flow.do: Your child chooses the best amount of water and adds one idea of their own. Make one more print and compare it with the best of the three.
flow.say: Now make your own best print. What will you change? Tell me why before you start.
flow.kid: Make your own best print. Change one thing. Say why first.
flow.parent: Praise a clear reason as much as a sharp print. Throw all leftover plaster in the dustbin, never in the sink.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Sharpest Coin Print. You design your own best plaster mix and test it.

items.p: What happens to the atoms in a chemical reaction?
items.why: A reaction breaks some bonds and makes new ones. Every atom is still there afterwards, joined to new partners.

items.p: Match each kind of reaction to its pattern.
pairs: One substance becomes two or more
items.why: Count the substances before and after. Two into one is joining, and one into two is splitting. An exchange is swapping. A fuel with oxygen is burning.

items.p: A solid that forms inside a liquid during a reaction is called a ____.
items.why: A precipitate forms when one product of a reaction does not dissolve in water. Curds in milk are a precipitate.

items.p: Plaster of Paris goes hard only because its water dries away.
items.why: False. Plaster joins with the water and makes a new solid. It is hard while it is still wet, and it stays hard in water.

items.p: Sort each reaction. Is it a joining or a splitting?
items: plaster of Paris and water become gypsum
iron, oxygen and water become rust
quicklime and water become slaked lime
heated baking soda becomes three substances
electricity turns water into hydrogen and oxygen
a heated seashell becomes quicklime and a gas
items.why: In a joining, there are fewer substances after the reaction than before. In a splitting, there are more.

items.p: Heat turns baking soda into washing soda and two other substances. Which two?
items.why: The water leaves as steam and can be caught on a cold lid. The carbon dioxide leaves as a gas you cannot see.

items.p: The thin, pale liquid left after curds come out of milk is called ____.
items.why: Whey is mostly water, with milk sugar and minerals. The curds hold most of the protein and fat.

items.p: Burning needs oxygen.
items.why: True. Burning is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen. A flame goes out when the oxygen around it runs low.

items.p: Vinegar is added to soap water. What do you see?
items.why: Soap and vinegar swap parts. One product is a waxy solid that does not dissolve, so the water turns milky.

items.p: Lemon juice is stirred into hot milk. Put what happens in order.
items: The acid cancels the charge on the casein clusters
The clusters stop repelling each other
a: The acid cancels the charge on the casein clusters
The clusters stop repelling each other
items.why: The charge keeps the clusters apart. Once the acid cancels it, they can stick together and come out as a solid.

items.p: More lemon juice is added to whey, and no new curds form. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: Curds are made from casein and acid. All the casein in the milk had already become curds, so the extra lemon juice had nothing to react with.
items.why: A strong answer names the reactant that was used up, the casein. It says that a reaction needs every reactant.

items.p: A cup of setting plaster feels warm. Where does the heat come from?
items.a: The plaster and the water join and make new bonds. Making bonds gives out energy, and we feel it as heat.
items.why: A strong answer says that a reaction is happening, and that making new bonds gives out energy.

items.p: Draw a swapping reaction with four shapes. Show the two substances before and the two substances after.
items.a: Before: two pairs of joined shapes, for example a circle with a square and a triangle with a star. After: the same four shapes in new pairs, such as the circle with the star and the triangle with the square.
items.why: A strong drawing uses the same four shapes before and after. Only the partners change.
items.art: A blank box divided in two by an arrow, with 'before' written on the left and 'after' on the right.

items.p: Is burning a splitting or a joining?

views.says: It is a splitting. A log becomes ash, smoke and gases. One thing becomes many things.
It is a joining. The atoms of the fuel join with oxygen from the air. A metal even gets heavier when it burns.
It is both. The bonds in the fuel break, and new bonds to oxygen form. That is why I give burning a name of its own.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about burning. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view can be argued well. The first child is right that the fuel comes apart. The second is right that oxygen is taken in. The chemist joins the two views.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the need for oxygen or the gases given off. It also answers another view fairly.

items.p: Which of these is a fuel?
items.why: Wax is made of carbon and hydrogen, which can join with oxygen. Water, sand and ash are already joined with oxygen.

items.p: Why do many splitting reactions need heat or electricity?
items.why: To split a substance, bonds must break, and that takes energy in. Heat and electricity supply the energy.

items.p: Why do casein clusters stay spread out in fresh milk?
opts: They carry the same charge and repel
They are too heavy to move
items.why: Charges of the same kind repel. Each cluster pushes the others away, so they stay spread through the milk.

items.p: A candle under a glass goes out while wax is still left. Which reactant ran low?
items.why: Burning needs fuel and oxygen. The glass keeps new air out, so the oxygen runs low and the flame stops.

items.p: In a swapping reaction, some atoms are destroyed.
items.why: False. The parts only change partners. Every atom that was there before is there afterwards.

items.p: Water does not burn, because its hydrogen has already joined with oxygen.
items.why: True. Water is what hydrogen becomes when it burns. It has no more joining with oxygen left to do.

items.p: Three of these are joining reactions. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Rusting, setting plaster and quicklime with water each make one substance from two or more. Soda goes flat when carbonic acid splits.

items.p: Methane (1 carbon atom, 4 hydrogen atoms) burns with 4 oxygen atoms. How many atoms are in the products?
items.why: 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 atoms before the reaction. A reaction keeps every atom, so there are 9 atoms in the products.

items.p: Sort each reaction. Does it give out heat, or does it need energy put in?
items.why: Making new bonds gives out energy, so joining and burning give out heat. Breaking bonds takes energy, so these splitting reactions need heat or electricity.

items.p: Lime for plaster starts as a seashell. Put the steps in order.
items: A kiln's heat splits the shell into quicklime and a gas
The wet lime is spread on a wall
The lime joins with carbon dioxide from the air and hardens
a: A kiln's heat splits the shell into quicklime and a gas
The wet lime is spread on a wall
The lime joins with carbon dioxide from the air and hardens
items.why: The shell is split once and then joins twice, first with water and then with carbon dioxide. At the end it is the same substance as the shell.

items.p: Whey stops making curds after a few spoons of fresh milk. Which reactant ran out? How do you know?
items.a: The acid ran out. The new milk still had casein in it, yet it stayed white. One more teaspoon of lemon juice made curds again.
items.why: A strong answer names the acid, and gives evidence: the milk stayed white, or more lemon brought the curds back.

items.p: A dry powder is heated, and water drops appear on a cold lid above it. What does this tell you?
items.a: The water came out of the powder. Heat split the powder into new substances, and one of them was water. An empty pan gives no drops, so the water did not come from the pan.
items.why: A strong answer says the powder was split, and uses the empty pan as the comparison.

items.p: Dish wash liquid still foams when vinegar is added, but soap does not. Explain the difference.
items.a: Soap swaps parts with the acid in vinegar and becomes a waxy solid that does not dissolve or foam. Dish wash liquid is made of different substances, which stay dissolved in sour water.
items.why: A strong answer says that the soap became a new substance, and that the dish wash liquid did not.

items.p: Milk left out overnight has turned sour and lumpy. Is that the same change as making paneer?

views.says: No. I make paneer on purpose, from fresh milk, and it is good to eat. Sour milk has gone bad.
Yes. In both, an acid makes the casein clump. In the old milk, bacteria made the acid.
The curdling is the same. But old milk may also hold bacteria who can make a person ill, so I treat the two differently.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about reactions. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view can be argued well. The reaction that makes the lumps is the same in both. What differs is where the acid came from, and what else is in the milk.
items.why: A strong answer separates the reaction from the question of safety, and uses what acid does to casein.

items.p: Label three parts of this word equation: plaster of Paris + water → gypsum.
a: Reactants: plaster of Paris and water, before the arrow
items.why: Reactants are what you start with, and they go before the arrow. Products are what the reaction makes, and they go after it.
items.art: The word equation 'plaster of Paris + water → gypsum' written large, with three blank label lines pointing at the left side, the arrow and the right side.

items.p: The reactant that runs out first, and so stops the reaction, is called the ____ reactant.
items.why: The limiting reactant sets how much product is made. Whatever is left of the other reactants stays unused.

items.p: Hydrogen burns with oxygen and makes only water. Which two kinds does this reaction fit?
items.why: A fuel reacts with oxygen, so it is burning. Two substances become one, so it is also a joining.

items.p: Vinegar and baking soda swap parts and then fizz. Which step makes the gas?
items.why: The swap makes carbonic acid. Carbonic acid then splits into water and carbon dioxide gas, which is the fizz.

items.p: People once said a burning thing loses a substance. Which finding does not fit that idea?
opts: Metals get heavier when they burn
Wood leaves a little light ash
items.why: A thing that only loses something cannot get heavier. Burning metals gain weight because they join with oxygen.

items.p: A mix holds twice the water that its plaster can join with. What happens to the extra water?
items.why: Plaster joins with a fixed amount of water. When the plaster is used up, the rest of the water is left over and dries away.

items.p: A swapping reaction can run backwards if one of its products is present in a huge amount.
items.why: True. Berthollet saw this at the salt lakes of Egypt. Amounts help to decide which way a reaction runs.

items.p: The Sun shines because hydrogen burns with oxygen inside it.
items.why: False. Inside the Sun, the centres of hydrogen atoms join. That is a nuclear reaction, and it needs no oxygen.

items.p: Match each everyday change to its kind of reaction.
pairs: A cake rises in the oven
A grey ring forms on a soapy bucket
A brass lamp slowly goes dark
items.why: Baking soda splits and gives off gas. Soap swaps sodium for calcium. Brass joins with gases from the air. Incense is a fuel reacting with oxygen.

items.p: 200 millilitres of milk needs 3 teaspoons of lemon juice to curdle. How many teaspoons does 1 litre need?
items.why: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres, which is 5 times 200. So it needs 5 times 3 teaspoons, which is 15.

items.p: Sunlight splits oxygen molecules high in the air. The atoms join other oxygen molecules and make ____.
items.why: Ozone has three oxygen atoms. A layer of it high in the air shields living beings from harsh sunlight.

items.p: Many people think a paste hardens only by drying. Describe a test that could show a reaction instead.
items.a: Mix the paste and check it while it is still wet. If it is hard and wet at once, it did not harden by drying. Also feel for warmth, and put the dry lump in water to see if it stays hard.
items.why: A strong answer names something to observe that drying cannot explain: hard while wet, warmth, or staying hard in water.

items.p: A cook adds lemon juice to hot milk, but the whey still looks milky. What should be added, and why?
items.a: More lemon juice. Milky whey still has casein in it, so the acid ran out first. More acid will turn the rest of the casein into curds.
items.why: A strong answer works out which reactant is left over, and adds the one that ran out.

items.p: Fresh quicklime gets hot in water. Quicklime kept in damp air for weeks does not. Explain why.
items.a: Quicklime gets hot because it joins with water. In damp air it joins slowly with water from the air. After some weeks none is left to join, so nothing happens in water.
items.why: A strong answer says that the joining has already happened, so the reactant is used up.

items.p: Your cells and a candle both turn fuel and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. Name one difference.
items.a: A candle does it fast, with a flame and a lot of heat at once. Cells do it in many small steps, with no flame, and keep much of the energy to use.
items.why: A strong answer compares speed, flame or steps. It does not say the two are unrelated.

items.p: Are the four kinds of reaction found in nature, or are they only a way of sorting?

views.says: They are real patterns. If I know the kind, I can often say what the products will be.
They are our sorting. Burning fits two kinds. I sort reactions by what moves between the substances.

views.who: A child who built reactions from seeds
views.says: On every plate I broke some bonds and made new ones. Perhaps there is only one kind.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about reactions. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view can be argued well. The patterns are real enough to predict products. Some reactions still fit two kinds, and other ways of sorting also work.
items.why: A strong answer gives an example reaction as evidence, and says what the sorting is useful for.

items.p: Draw milk before and after lemon juice, as a very strong microscope would show it. Show the casein clusters.
items.a: Before: many small round clusters spread evenly, each with the same charge sign. After: the clusters stuck together in a few big lumps, with clear liquid between them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same clusters before and after. They are spread out at first and clumped afterwards.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, labelled 'milk' and 'milk with lemon juice'.

quiz.p: Which pattern shows a joining reaction?
quiz.why: In a joining, two substances become one. The second pattern is a splitting and the third is a swapping.

quiz.p: One substance breaks into two or more new substances. What kind of reaction is this?
quiz.why: One substance becoming two or more is a splitting. Heated baking soda does this.

quiz.p: What does burning need, besides a fuel and some heat to start?
quiz.why: Burning is a fuel reacting with oxygen. Water and carbon dioxide are what burning makes.

quiz.p: Why does lemon juice make curds in hot milk?
opts: Acid makes casein clusters stick together
quiz.why: The acid cancels the charge that keeps the casein clusters apart. They stick together and come out as curds.

quiz.p: Plaster of Paris sets hard while it is still wet. What happened to the water?
quiz.why: Plaster and water join and make one new solid. The water is locked inside the solid.

quiz.p: A reaction stops, although plenty of one reactant is left. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The other reactant is used up
quiz.why: A reaction needs every reactant. When one is used up, the reaction stops, however much of the other is left.

quiz.p: Soap and vinegar make a white solid and a dissolved salt. What kind of reaction is this?
quiz.why: Two substances exchange parts and make two new substances. The sodium and the hydrogen change places.

quiz.p: In a chemical reaction, atoms are made and destroyed.
quiz.why: False. Atoms are only rearranged. The same atoms are there before and after.

quiz.p: Which of these will not burn in a candle flame?
quiz.why: Ash is what is left after burning. Its atoms have already joined with oxygen.

quiz.p: Dry baking soda is heated, and drops of water collect on a cold lid. Where did the water come from?
opts: From the baking soda as it split
From the steel of the lid
From the air in the kitchen
quiz.why: Heat splits baking soda into washing soda, water and carbon dioxide. The water leaves as steam and turns to drops on the cold lid.

quiz.p: Which reaction fits two kinds at once?
quiz.why: Hydrogen burning is a fuel reacting with oxygen, and it is two substances becoming one. The other three are not chemical reactions.

opts: A solid formed inside a liquid
A gas that escapes from a liquid
A liquid that dissolves a solid
A powder that is stirred into water
quiz.why: A precipitate is a new solid that appears inside a liquid, because one product does not dissolve.

applications: Paneer and cheese makers add an acid or an enzyme to milk. They measure it, so that all the casein becomes curds and little acid is left over.
Doctors set broken bones in casts of plaster of Paris. The wet bandage joins with water and turns hard within minutes.
Bakers use baking soda because heat splits it and gives off carbon dioxide. The gas makes cakes, dhoklas and biscuits rise.
Water works add alum to muddy water. The alum forms a fluffy precipitate, which traps the fine mud and sinks. The clear water is drawn off the top.
Shampoos and dish wash liquids were invented because soap swaps parts with hard water and makes scum. These cleaners do not make scum, because they stay dissolved in hard water.
Engines and stoves are built to mix fuel with enough oxygen. With too little oxygen, burning makes soot and a poisonous gas called carbon monoxide.

open_questions.q: Which chemical reactions first led to life on the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: No one was there to see it, and the first reactions left no fossils. Scientists test ideas in the laboratory, but no one has yet made life from simple chemicals.

open_questions.q: How exactly are the casein clusters in milk built?
open_questions.why_open: The clusters are too small and too soft to see clearly. Dairy scientists have several models of them, and they still disagree.

open_questions.q: Can we split carbon dioxide cheaply, using only sunlight, as a leaf does?
open_questions.why_open: Leaves do it at ordinary temperatures. Laboratories can copy parts of it, but the methods are still slow or costly.

open_questions.q: Can a computer predict the products of any reaction before it is tried?
open_questions.why_open: Computers do well for small molecules. For large ones, the sums are too big, and the answer often has to be found by experiment.

open_questions.q: What happens during the instant when a bond is half broken?
open_questions.why_open: Very short laser flashes can now catch molecules in the middle of reacting. Only a few simple reactions have been followed in this way.

maths.problem: In Second Squeeze, 200 millilitres of hot milk needed 3 teaspoons of lemon juice to make curds. How many teaspoons would 600 millilitres of the same milk need?
maths.explain: 600 millilitres is 3 times 200 millilitres. So it holds 3 times as much casein, and needs 3 times 3 teaspoons, which is 9.
maths.context: In Second Squeeze you add lemon juice to hot milk, one teaspoon at a time, until curds and whey form. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Reactants are used in fixed amounts. Multiplying tells a cook how much lemon juice a bigger pot of milk will need.

maths.problem: In Second Squeeze, a tumbler with 5 tablespoons of whey made curds from 4 tablespoons of milk. The 5th tablespoon stayed white. What would happen with 10 tablespoons of the same whey?
maths.answer: About 8 tablespoons of milk would make curds, and the 9th would stay white.
maths.explain: 10 tablespoons of whey hold twice as much leftover acid as 5. Each tablespoon of milk uses up the same amount of acid. So twice as much milk can be curdled: 2 times 4 is 8.
maths.context: In Second Squeeze you add hot milk to leftover whey, one tablespoon at a time, until the milk stays white. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning with the numbers lets you predict a test before you do it. Then the test can check your idea about the leftover acid.

maths.problem: A chemist heats 84 grams of baking soda until it has all split. 53 grams of washing soda are left in the pan. How many grams left the pan as water and carbon dioxide?
maths.explain: No atom is lost in a reaction. So the products together weigh 84 grams. 84 − 53 = 31 grams left as steam and gas.
maths.context: In The Pan and the Lid, heat splits baking soda into washing soda, water and carbon dioxide. The water and the gas leave the pan.
maths.why_maths: You cannot catch and weigh the gas at home. Subtracting tells you its weight, because the total weight never changes.

maths.problem: In The Sharpest Coin Print, the best mix was 2 tablespoons of plaster to 1 tablespoon of water. A sculptor uses 9 tablespoons of water. How much plaster does she need?
maths.explain: The plaster is always 2 times the water. 2 times 9 is 18.
maths.context: In The Sharpest Coin Print you make plaster mixes with different amounts of water. You find which one copies a coin best.
maths.why_maths: Plaster joins with a fixed share of water. A ratio keeps that share the same for a small cast or a large one.

maths.problem: In Soap and Sour, the foam in bottle A was 4 cm and then 4 cm. In bottle C it was 3 cm and then 3.5 cm. In bottle B it was 0.5 cm both times. Can you be sure that A foams more than C? Can you be sure that A foams more than B?
maths.answer: Yes, you can be sure that A foams more than B. No, you cannot be sure that A foams more than C from these tries alone.
maths.explain: A's foam is 8 times as tall as B's, and both tries agree. A and C differ by only 0.5 to 1 cm. C's own two tries differ from each other by 0.5 cm. So the gap between A and C is not much bigger than the gap between two tries of the same bottle. That gap could be chance.
maths.context: In Soap and Sour you shake soap water with plain water in bottle A and with vinegar in bottle B. Bottle C holds dish wash liquid with vinegar. These are made-up foam heights.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a difference with the spread between repeated tries tells you whether the difference is real.

maths.problem: The table shows the four reactions from Four Plates. Which number is the same before and after on every plate? Which number can change?
maths.answer: The number of atoms never changes. The number of molecules can change.
maths.explain: Atoms: 6 and 6, 6 and 6, 5 and 5, 9 and 9. Molecules: 2 become 1 in the joining, and 1 becomes 2 in the splitting. In the swapping and the burning the count of molecules happens to stay the same.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, chemists thought that each substance has a fixed liking for every other substance. A substance that likes a partner more would pull it away from a substance that likes it less. In 1775 the Swedish chemist Torbern Bergman printed large tables of these likings. By this idea, a swap could go only one way. In 1798 the French chemist Claude-Louis Berthollet went to Egypt. At the Natron Lakes he saw crusts of soda at the edges of the salt water. The ground there was limestone. In his laboratory, soda and a dissolved lime salt always swapped parts, and made limestone and common salt. At the lakes, salt and limestone were slowly making soda. The swap was running backwards. Berthollet reasoned that the huge amount of salt was driving it. Amounts matter, as well as likes. He published the idea in 1801 and 1803. He also claimed that substances join in any proportions. Joseph Proust showed that this part was wrong. In 1864 Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage in Norway turned Berthollet's idea into an exact rule.
how_we_found_out.who: Torbern Bergman in Sweden, Claude-Louis Berthollet and Joseph Proust from France, and Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage in Norway
how_we_found_out.when: Bergman's tables came out in 1775. Berthollet was in Egypt from 1798 to 1799, and published in 1801 and 1803. Guldberg and Waage published in 1864.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That each substance has fixed likes, so a swapping reaction can go only one way. Berthollet saw the same swap running backwards at the Natron Lakes, where one substance was present in a huge amount.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in late eighteenth-century clothes kneeling at the edge of a desert salt lake, lifting a white crust from the shore, with limestone rocks behind him.

roots.context: In this unit you sorted reactions into four kinds: joining, splitting, swapping and burning. Here we ask what is the same under all four.

deep_truth.truth: In The Pan and the Lid, heat broke bonds in baking soda, and one powder became three substances. In Powder and Water, plaster and water made new bonds and became one hard solid. In Soap and Sour, old bonds broke and new bonds formed in the same bottle. So every reaction, whatever its kind, is made of the same two steps: bonds break and bonds form.
deep_truth.habit: We sort reactions into kinds, and then we treat the kinds as separate things. The kinds are patterns that people noticed. Under every pattern, the same two steps are happening.
deep_truth.evidence: In Four Plates, every reaction was built by pulling some seeds apart and pushing some together. The burning plate needed both steps. In the card game Join, Split, Swap or Burn, three cards fit two kinds at once. That happens because every kind is made of the same two steps.

three.who_am_i: The calcium in your bones was once in milk, in grass, in soil and in rock. It has changed partners many times, and for now it is part of you.
three.what_is_life: A living being keeps thousands of joining, splitting and swapping reactions going at once. A clam building a shell and a child digesting lunch are both doing chemistry.
three.what_is_this_world: About ninety kinds of atom are found in nature. Breaking bonds and making bonds is enough to turn them into milk, stone, flame and you.

roots.thread: A seashell, a lump of lime, a plastered wall and a stalactite all hold calcium atoms, with different partners. Reactions move atoms from one substance to another, and nothing is added or lost on the way. Many sages taught that the many things of the world are forms of one source. The science here says something close and plain. All substances are built from the same few kinds of atom. Old bonds break and new bonds form, and that is how one substance becomes another.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Empedocles said that all things are made of a few lasting 'roots'. At one time they grow together into one, and at another time they grow apart into many.
teachings.link: This is joining and splitting, said 2,400 years ago. His four roots were earth, water, air and fire, which are not the elements of chemistry. But his idea that change is lasting parts coming together and apart is what chemists later found.
verse: δίπλ’ ἐρέω· τοτὲ μὲν γὰρ ἕν ηὐξήθη μόνον εἶναι
ἐκ πλεόνων, τοτὲ δ’ αὖ διέφυ πλέον’ ἐξ ἑνὸς εἶναι
